pos: n. (proper name; mother of king Josiah)
etymology: Hebrew Yedidah, beloved, from yadid, beloved, the same root as Jedidiah, the LORD's name for Solomon.
biblical_def: Jedidah is the mother of Josiah, the most thoroughly reforming king of Judah. “Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty and one years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Jedidah, the daughter of Adaiah of Boscath” (2 Kings 22:1). Her husband was Amon, who “forsook the LORD God of his fathers” and was murdered after two years; her son came to the throne a child. The verdict on him is unique: “like unto him was there no king before him, that turned to the LORD with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might” (2 Kings 23:25). Scripture does not say what Jedidah taught him, but it places her name at the head of his reign, and the boy who grew up in the house of an idolatrous father “while he was yet young, he began to seek after the God of David his father” (2 Chronicles 34:3). The beloved mother of a king who turned wholly to the LORD stands as a quiet witness to the godly woman's hidden work.

corruption_paragraphs: Modern culture measures a woman's worth by career and public influence and treats the raising of children as secondary. Scripture names the mothers of the kings because the formation of a son is a work of the first importance.

pos: n. (proper name; mother of king Joash of Judah)
biblical_def: Zibiah of Beersheba is the mother of Joash, the boy-king hidden in the temple from Athaliah. “In the seventh year of Jehu Jehoash began to reign; and forty years reigned he in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Zibiah of Beersheba” (2 Kings 12:1). Chronicles repeats her name (2 Chronicles 24:1). She was a wife of Ahaziah, and when Athaliah destroyed the royal seed, her infant son was stolen away by Jehosheba and kept six years in the house of the LORD. Zibiah came from Beersheba, at the southern edge of the land. Her son's reign was good while he had a teacher: “Jehoash did that which was right in the sight of the LORD all his days wherein Jehoiada the priest instructed him” (2 Kings 12:2). After Jehoiada died, Joash turned to idols and slew Jehoiada's son Zechariah. The record of Zibiah's son warns that borrowed faith does not last; a man must have the LORD for himself.

pos: n. (proper name; mother of king Jehoiachin)
biblical_def: Nehushta is the queen mother who went into captivity with her son Jehoiachin. “Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem three months. And his mother's name was Nehushta, the daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem” (2 Kings 24:8). Her father Elnathan was a prince of Jehoiakim's court. The reign lasted three months, and “he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his father had done” (2 Kings 24:9). Then “Jehoiachin the king of Judah went out to the king of Babylon, he, and his mother” (2 Kings 24:12). Nebuchadnezzar “carried away Jehoiachin to Babylon, and the king's mother, and the king's wives” (2 Kings 24:15). Jeremiah had spoken directly to her: “Say unto the king and to the queen, Humble yourselves, sit down” (Jeremiah 13:18). Her name means bronze; her crown fell. The queen mother who shared the throne shared its judgment.

pos: n. (proper name; mother of king Jotham)
etymology: Hebrew Yerusha, possession, inheritance, from yarash, to possess, to inherit.
biblical_def: Jerusha the daughter of Zadok is the mother of Jotham, king of Judah. “Five and twenty years old was he when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Jerusha, the daughter of Zadok” (2 Kings 15:33). Chronicles spells her Jerushah (2 Chronicles 27:1). Her father Zadok may have been of the priestly line. She was the wife of Uzziah, the leper king, and her son ruled in his father's stead during his illness. Jotham's verdict is among the best in Kings: “he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD: he did according to all that his father Uzziah had done” (2 Kings 15:34), and Chronicles adds that he did not enter the temple as his father had. “So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the LORD his God” (2 Chronicles 27:6). Yet “the high places were not removed” (2 Kings 15:35). Jerusha's son was faithful in his own walk but did not reform the people.

pos: n. (proper name; mother of king Uzziah)
etymology: Hebrew Yekolyah, the LORD is able, from yakol, to be able, and Yah; spelled Jecholiah in 2 Kings 15:2.
biblical_def: Jecoliah of Jerusalem is the mother of Uzziah, also called Azariah. “Sixteen years old was Uzziah when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty and two years in Jerusalem. His mother's name also was Jecoliah of Jerusalem” (2 Chronicles 26:3). Kings spells her name Jecholiah (2 Kings 15:2). She was the wife of Amaziah. Her son's long reign was the high noon of Judah after Solomon: “as long as he sought the LORD, God made him to prosper” (2 Chronicles 26:5). Her name confesses that the LORD is able, and the early reign proved it. But prosperity became a snare: “when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction” (2 Chronicles 26:16), and Uzziah went into the temple to burn incense, which belonged to the priests alone. He was struck with leprosy and died a leper. The son of a mother whose name praised God's ability fell by trusting his own.

pos: n. (proper name; mother of king Amon)
etymology: Hebrew Meshullemeth, recompensed or friend, from shalam, to be whole, to repay.
biblical_def: Meshullemeth is the wife of Manasseh and mother of Amon. “Amon was twenty and two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Meshullemeth, the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah” (2 Kings 21:19). She married the king who filled Jerusalem with idols and innocent blood. Manasseh repented late in life, but his son learned the sins and not the repentance: “he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, as his father Manasseh did” (2 Kings 21:20). “And he forsook the LORD God of his fathers, and walked not in the way of the LORD” (2 Kings 21:22). After two years “the servants of Amon conspired against him, and slew the king in his own house” (2 Kings 21:23). Meshullemeth came from Jotbah, probably in Galilee, far from Jerusalem. Her son's brief reign is the darkness just before the dawn of Josiah, her grandson.

pos: n. (proper name; mother of king Amaziah)
etymology: Hebrew Yeho'addan, the LORD is delight, from Yah and 'adan, to delight.
biblical_def: Jehoaddan of Jerusalem is the mother of Amaziah, king of Judah. “He was twenty and five years old when he began to reign, and reigned twenty and nine years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Jehoaddan of Jerusalem” (2 Kings 14:2). Chronicles gives the same words (2 Chronicles 25:1). She was a wife of Joash. Amaziah's verdict is carefully qualified: “he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, yet not like David his father” (2 Kings 14:3), and Chronicles is sharper, “but not with a perfect heart” (2 Chronicles 25:2). He defeated Edom, then brought the gods of Edom home and bowed to them, and was defeated by Israel and later murdered. Jehoaddan's name means the LORD is delight; her son's heart delighted in Him only in part. The divided heart is the lesson of his reign.

pos: n. (proper name; a daughter of Solomon)
etymology: Hebrew Taphath, a drop, from nataph, to drop, to distil.
biblical_def: Taphath is a daughter of Solomon, married to one of his twelve district officers. “And Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, which provided victuals for the king and his household: each man his month in a year made provision” (1 Kings 4:7). Among them was “The son of Abinadab, in all the region of Dor; which had Taphath the daughter of Solomon to wife” (1 Kings 4:11). Her sister Basmath married Ahimaaz, another officer. Solomon bound his administration together by marriage, and the son of Abinadab may have been his nephew. Taphath appears only here, in the record of Solomon's peace, when “Judah and Israel dwelt safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, from Dan even to Beersheba, all the days of Solomon” (1 Kings 4:25). Her name, a drop, is a small thing in a great kingdom, yet the Spirit recorded it in the chapter that describes Israel's fullest earthly glory, a picture of the greater kingdom of the Son of David.

pos: n. (proper name; daughter of Haran, sister of Milcah and Lot)
etymology: Hebrew Yiskah, perhaps she will look or observant, from sakah, to look.
biblical_def: Iscah is the daughter of Haran, Abram's brother, named once in the genealogy of Terah. “Now these are the generations of Terah: Terah begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran; and Haran begat Lot” (Genesis 11:27). Then: “the name of Nahor's wife, Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah, and the father of Iscah” (Genesis 11:29). She was thus sister to Milcah and to Lot. Jewish tradition identified Iscah with Sarai, but Scripture does not: Sarai is named separately in the same verse, and Abraham later says of her, “she is the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother” (Genesis 20:12), which a daughter of Haran could not be. Iscah's name stands without a story. The genealogy moves on to the barren Sarai and the call of Abram, through whom all the families of the earth would be blessed. Iscah reminds the reader that God's choice of one line was made from among many named and real persons.

pos: n. (proper name; Hittite wife of Esau)
etymology: Hebrew Yehudith, Jewess or praised, feminine of Yehudah, Judah, praise.
biblical_def: Judith is the Hittite woman whom Esau married against the wishes of his parents. “And Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite” (Genesis 26:34). The next verse gives the verdict: “Which were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah” (Genesis 26:35). Abraham had sworn his servant not to take a wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites, and Esau ignored the covenant line's concern for a believing marriage. Rebekah afterward said, “I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth” (Genesis 27:46), and sent Jacob to Haran for a wife. Esau, “seeing that the daughters of Canaan pleased not Isaac his father” (Genesis 28:8), added a daughter of Ishmael, but did not put away the Hittites. Judith is distinct from the heroine of the apocryphal Book of Judith, which is no part of the canon. Esau's marriages show the profane man who despised his birthright despising also the holy line.
